Why this matters

From the screen to the world

Every program you've written so far has lived inside a screen. Physical computing breaks the glass. The Raspberry Pi 5 is a full Linux computer the size of a credit card with a row of pins — its GPIO header — that can switch real voltage on and off thousands of times a second. Your Python becomes light, motion, and sound.

It's the same chip running behind smart doorbells, retro game emulators, weather stations, robot rovers, 3D-printer farms and the high-altitude balloons students launch to the edge of space. Learn it here, then build it for real on the classroom Pi fleet.

Hardware brief

Meet the Raspberry Pi 5

A single-board computer (SBC): a complete computer — CPU, RAM, USB, networking, video — on one board. What makes it special for us is the 40-pin GPIO header along one edge. Hover any pin below to learn its job.

RASPBERRY PI 5 · 40-PIN GPIO HEADER · (BCM numbering)
Power (3V3/5V) Ground (GND) GPIO (general use) I²C / SPI / UART PWM-capable
Physical vs BCM: Pins also have a physical number (1–40, the position on the header). In Python with gpiozero we almost always use the BCM/GPIO number — e.g. LED(17) means BCM GPIO 17, which is physical pin 11.
Hover a pin →

Move your mouse over any pin on the header to see its number, function, safe use and a code hint.

Pi 5 reality check: The Pi 5 uses a new RP1 I/O chip, so the old RPi.GPIO library no longer works the classic way. The modern, correct choice on a Pi 5 (Raspberry Pi OS or Kali) is the gpiozero library, which talks to the pins through the lgpio backend. Everything in this lab teaches the gpiozero way.
Golden safety rule: GPIO pins run at 3.3 V, not 5 V, and can only supply a tiny current (~16 mA). Always use a resistor with an LED, and never feed 5 V back into a GPIO input — it can kill the pin.
Coding the pins

Python + GPIO with gpiozero

gpiozero was built to make hardware readable. You describe what a thing is and the library handles the messy electronics. Here's the anatomy of the classic "Hello World" of hardware — the blinking LED.

Before you start — one-time setup on your Raspberry Pi 5

Open a Terminal on the Pi and install the libraries. The Pi 5 talks to its pins through the lgpio backend, so install that too. These steps work whether your Pi 5 runs Raspberry Pi OS or Kali Linux.

Raspberry Pi OS (Bookworm)
# gpiozero + lgpio ship with the OS, but make sure they're current
sudo apt update
sudo apt install -y python3-gpiozero python3-lgpio
Kali Linux (on the Pi 5)
# Kali doesn't ship them — install with apt (preferred)
sudo apt update
sudo apt install -y python3-gpiozero python3-lgpio

# ...or, inside a virtual environment, with pip:
pip install gpiozero lgpio
Why lgpio? The Pi 5's new RP1 I/O chip isn't supported by the old RPi.GPIO. Every lab below starts by pinning the lgpio backend explicitly: 
from gpiozero import LED, Device
from gpiozero.pins.lgpio import LGPIOFactory

Device.pin_factory = LGPIOFactory()   # Pi 5: same on Raspberry Pi OS & Kali
That one line makes the identical program run on both operating systems — no per-OS edits.
Run a program: save it as e.g. blink.py, then in the Terminal: python3 blink.py. Press Ctrl+C to stop a forever-loop.
Anatomy of a blink
# import the tools we need
from gpiozero import LED
from time import sleep

# create an LED object on GPIO 17
led = LED(17)

while True:        # repeat forever
    led.on()       # 3.3V — light ON
    sleep(1)        # wait 1 second
    led.off()      # 0V — light OFF
    sleep(1)        # wait 1 second

Four ideas power almost everything: import a device class, create an object tied to a pin, call methods on it (.on(), .off()), and control timing with sleep() and loops.

Two ways to "talk" to a pin

Digital — ON or OFF

led.on() / led.off(). The pin is either 3.3 V (1) or 0 V (0). Perfect for switching things hard on and off.

PWM — anywhere in between

Pulse-Width Modulation flicks the pin on/off so fast your eyes see a dimmed light or a motor at half speed. PWMLED(17).value = 0.5 = 50% brightness.

The water analogy (carried over from CIRCUIT FORGE)

Voltage = water pressure (the Pi pushes at 3.3 V). Current = how much water flows. A resistor is a narrow section of pipe that limits the flow so your LED doesn't burn out.

Inputs vs Outputs

Outputs (LED, Buzzer, Motor, Servo) — the Pi pushes voltage out to make things happen.
Inputs (Button, LDR, PIR, Ultrasonic) — the Pi listens for a voltage coming in and reads the world.

Your programs almost always follow the loop: read inputs → decide → drive outputs → repeat. That's robotics in one sentence.
